dimensions.name: Understanding the LSP contract & golden output format

evidence.note: Systematic upfront orientation: read run_tests.sh and score_golden.py, inspected golden.jsonl, enumerated methods by frequency, and derived key contract facts (empty didOpen text ⇒ read from disk, basename URIs, line/character positions, tree-sitter node types) before committing to implementation.

Extracted concrete exemplars to distinguish three distinct name-format conventions across documentSymbol (types only), hover (types+names), and prepareCallHierarchy (types + ':' return) — building an explicit per-method format spec.
Dissected the scorer's normalize/compare logic to understand hover-text vs JSON comparison and folding order-sensitivity — deriving format requirements from the harness itself, not guessing.
Verified 0-indexing and exact range boundaries by counting columns against golden character offsets — pinning down subtle indexing/URI/range details.

Re-probed the data whenever a mismatch revealed a misunderstood contract detail: found references≠documentHighlight ranges, Constructor-vs-Type query asymmetry, and that compareTo Javadoc only applies under @Override — sustained self-correcting inquiry.
Distinguished format requirements (fixable) from hard semantic requirements (argument-type inference for overloads) rather than conflating them — hallmark of the level-10 anchor.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent treated golden.jsonl as an explicit reverse-engineering target: it read run_tests and the scorer, enumerated methods, extracted concrete exemplars, and derived per-method invariants (formats, 0-indexing, URI basename, range boundaries, ranges differing across methods), cross-checking against JDT-LS conventions and re-probing on every mismatch. This inquiry was sustained across the entire 235-step build, not just the opening — matching the level-10 description almost point for point.

dimensions.name: Layering the build (lexer → parser → AST → analysis → per-method handlers)

evidence.note: Foundation-first ordering: explored workspace, golden format, method distribution, network/crate availability, and tree-sitter grammar node types BEFORE writing code. This is a deliberate de-risking spike into the highest-risk area (exact JDT-LS output shape and parser choice) prior to committing to the build.

Explicit layered architecture: main.rs (protocol/dispatch plumbing), analyzer.rs (tree-sitter parsing + symbol model), methods.rs (per-method handlers). Got a build passing, then ran run_tests for a 41% baseline — a concrete done-check establishing that the plumbing+parse layers minimally work before per-method refinement.

Method-by-method sequence explicitly prioritized by cost-to-pass / leverage: repeatedly listed per-method pass rates and picked 'biggest wins' or 'lowest %' next (e.g. foldingRange 0%→99%, then references, documentHighlight). Each method had a concrete check — its pass rate after each change — and the plan was revisited as passing counts revealed where remaining value concentrated.

Leverage/risk triage sustained to the end: deliberately skipped semanticTokens ('hard to match without exact legend') as too costly, and reverted changes (steps 234-235) that lowered aggregate score. Shows plan continually adjusted by where value concentrates rather than grinding.

Recognized shared machinery across method groups: references and documentHighlight share effective_range/roles_match logic; changes to one were consciously made conditional to avoid regressing the other — evidence of batching handlers by shared capability.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent exhibits the full anchor-8 pattern: an explicit milestone hierarchy (protocol dispatch → tree-sitter parse/symbol model → per-method handlers), a prioritized method sequence chosen by cost-to-pass, and a concrete done-check per milestone (pass rate after each run_tests). It also shows several anchor-10 traits — a genuine up-front de-risking spike into the riskiest area (exact golden format), reprioritization by leverage as pass counts shift, and batching methods by shared machinery. It falls short of a clean 10 because the initial build was somewhat all-at-once (all three modules stubbed before any validation) and later prioritization was largely reactive/emergent rather than a pre-sequenced risk plan. Solid 8.

dimensions.name: Driving development with the golden test loop and finer checks

evidence.note: Built /tmp/debug.py, a reusable per-method expected-vs-actual diff tool, immediately after the first run_tests baseline — verification infrastructure, not ad hoc checking.
Used run_tests as a steady outer loop, each time reading a per-method pass-rate breakdown to decide where to focus next.
Pinpointed exact divergent fields/positions (specific column offsets, missing selectionRange parent layer, enum_constant node) via per-triple diffing — far beyond an aggregate score.
Detected regressions caused by fixes (e.g. documentHighlight 70→42, documentSymbol 94.7%→68%) and reverted — regression guarding through the re-run loop.
Inspected the scorer's normalize/hover-extraction logic to understand whether format vs content matters, guarding against false passes.

Hardcoded Javadoc strings to match golden (a coincidental-format shortcut, self-limited via @Override), and only a single manual stdio invocation as a final crash check — the gaps keeping this short of a perfect 10.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent engineered a diffing tool (debug.py) used continuously to isolate single methods/files and pinpoint the exact divergent field or position, drove development with run_tests as the outer loop reading per-method rates, and repeatedly caught and reverted regressions — this squarely satisfies the level-8 anchor and reaches most of level 10 (structured diffing, regression detection, per-triple minimal reproduction sustained across the whole suite). It falls just shy of 10 because regression 'guarding' is via re-running aggregate per-method rates rather than a dedicated frozen check set, and it partly leans on hardcoded Javadoc format-matching, so I place it at 9.

dimensions.name: Tracking pass-rate across many methods without losing the plot

evidence.note: From the first test run the agent established a per-method breakdown ('41% baseline. Definition is 99.8%! Hover at 15.7%, prepareCallHierarchy 8.9%, foldingRange 0%, selectionRange 10%, references 37%') and continuously reported the aggregate plus per-method percentages after each change (61%, 66%), targeting the lowest-scoring methods.

Detected a regression promptly: 'documentHighlight regressed from 70 to 42 because we changed range,' diagnosed the cause (highlight wants name-only range vs references wanting name+args), and reverted — showing regression accounting at the per-method level.

Caught a large regression immediately ('documentSymbol dropped from 94.7% to 68%! Lots of regressions'), diagnosed nested vs anonymous class container mismatch, reverted and re-fixed, recovering to 95.1%.

Near the end recognized diminishing returns ('Marginal gains'), targeted the lowest method (references 87.6%), tried a scoped-resolution fix, saw it 'Made things worse,' reverted to 95.48%, and produced a full final per-method ledger (codeLens 99.4%, references 87.6%, semanticTokens 0%, typeDefinition 100%, etc.).
Maintained global-target awareness throughout ('gone from 41% -> 95.5%', 'reward requires 100%') while continuing to work local failures, and closed with an accurate 65106/68186 accounting.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept a live, per-method/per-file ledger of pass rates from the first test run to the last, re-checking after nearly every change; it detected multiple regressions promptly (documentHighlight 70→42, documentSymbol 94.7→68%, references worsening) and reverted each, and it recognized when edits produced only marginal movement and redirected to the lowest-scoring methods — behavior squarely at the level-8 anchor and reaching toward 10 by consistently prioritizing remaining work by weakest method while never losing the global 'all tests pass' target. It falls short of a clean 10 only because prioritization was heuristic (attack the lowest-percentage method) rather than explicitly reasoned by expected test-point gain, and some circling on documentHighlight/references persisted. Level 9 best fits the sustained, self-correcting accounting across the entire long horizon.

dimensions.name: Rearchitecting when the parser/analysis approach stalls

evidence.note: Foundational build-vs-reuse decision (adopt tree-sitter-java rather than hand-roll a parser) made once at the start; it proved sound and never stalled, so no big parser pivot was ever forced.

After changing method-call range to name+args, documentHighlight regressed 70→42 while references improved. Agent recognized the two methods need different ranges and reverted documentHighlight only — asymmetric handling rather than repeating one edit.

Type/Constructor role-matching helped references but hurt documentHighlight; agent made the matching conditional per-method rather than layering a hack — recognizing a shared resolution-model choice as root cause.

Reworked the symbol model to carry multiple representations (param types vs named params vs type-params; $-separated vs plain container) when it discovered one field couldn't serve documentSymbol, hover, and prepareCallHierarchy — a genuine serialization-model rework with dependent updates.

Repeated pattern of diagnosing regressions from failing evidence (wrong role variable passed; over-broad containerName change dropping documentSymbol 94.7→68; scoped-field resolution making things worse) and cleanly reverting or narrowing — preserves already-passing behavior.
semanticTokens left at 0% as a deliberate effort-allocation skip rather than rearchitected — a reasonable call but not an architectural pivot, capping the level below the highest anchors.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent never faced a falsified foundational bet: the tree-sitter reuse choice worked from the start, so the dramatic parser/architecture pivots described at level 10 never occurred and one method (semanticTokens) was abandoned rather than reworked. But it clearly exceeds level 5 'materially different tactic': it repeatedly diagnoses regressions from test evidence and reworks shared design decisions — the symbol model's container/param representations and the role-parameterized range/serialization logic (the level-8 'response serialization' example) — updating dependents rather than patching locally, while reliably reverting changes that hurt already-passing methods. That places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 6.

dimensions.name: Build-vs-reuse and effort allocation across a huge surface

evidence.note: Conscious build/reuse decision: checks cargo/network, then chooses tree-sitter-java for parsing and serde_json for JSON while hand-writing the LSP plumbing — an explicit choice to not hand-build a Java grammar. Plumbing choice is made but lightly rationalized.
Inspects tree-sitter-java node-types.json to stand on the parser crate's grammar, confirming reuse of the ecosystem piece for parsing.
Concentrates all hand-built effort on the semantic analysis layer (analyzer.rs/methods.rs) that earns test passes, keeping the solution a genuine AST analyzer atop the reused parser.
Deliberately deprioritizes semanticTokens ('Hard to match...Let me skip this'), allocating finite effort to higher-yield methods — effort allocation across the huge surface.

Hits tree-sitter's syntactic-only ceiling (needs type inference for overloads); recognizes the limit and shifts to heuristics/skips or reverts rather than grinding — but never revisits the build-vs-reuse tooling choice itself.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent makes a clear, sound build/reuse split (level 5) and goes further by deliberately allocating effort: leveraging tree-sitter for parsing and serde_json for JSON, while concentrating hand-built work on the AST analysis that earns passes and steering effort toward high-yield methods (level 8's core). However, the full level-8/10 behavior of revisiting the tooling choice when a dependency proves limiting is only partial — on hitting tree-sitter's semantic ceiling it re-allocates effort (skips/heuristics) but never reconsiders the tool leverage itself. That places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 7.

dimensions.name: Keeping the solution a real LSP, not a golden lookup

evidence.note: Committed to a genuinely general design: tree-sitter-java parsing plus separate analyzer/methods modules that read files from disk and answer via AST node analysis — a real LSP, not a lookup table.

Repeatedly derived general rules (method-overload signature/arity matching, role classification, scoped variable/field resolution) by studying examples then encoding general logic — consistent with a general analyzer rather than per-case answers.

Clear memorization slip: explicitly HARDCODES inherited Javadoc strings for Object/Iterator/Iterable methods ('I could hardcode these', 'gives us ~400 more passes') to force particular golden hover cases to pass — special-casing with memorized content, matching anchor 3.

Reverts changes when tests drop and gates the Javadoc hardcode behind @Override to reduce false positives, but all self-correction is driven by pass-rate, not by explicit reasoning about generality on untested inputs.
Never used golden.jsonl as a retrieval layer at runtime; final binary genuinely analyzes AST, and agent frames remaining gap as 'exact JDT-LS replication' rather than resorting to memorized answers.

dimensions.reasoning: The core solution is a genuinely general AST-based LSP that avoids runtime golden retrieval, which satisfies much of anchor 5, and it lacks explicit self-verification of generality (also consistent with 5's caveat). But the agent slips by hardcoding specific inherited-Javadoc strings to force particular golden hover cases (anchor 3's 'case-specific shortcuts/special-casing') and shows no principled guard against memorization — treating hardcoding as a legitimate pass-gaining tactic. This places it between anchors 3 and 5, at 4.

rubric.task_read: Build a real Java LSP server in Rust from scratch: a lexer/parser producing a Java AST, semantic analysis, and JSON-RPC-over-stdio handling for multiple LSP methods, scored against golden.jsonl triples derived from JDT-LS with an explicit 'no retrieval / all tests must pass' bar. This is an extremely long-horizon, high-complexity task with a huge implementation surface (Java grammar, symbol resolution, per-method response shapes that must byte-match another server's output). It rewards heavy, sustained meta-work: deep orientation into the LSP contract and the exact golden format, aggressive decomposition per method, a tight run_tests verification loop, continuous progress accounting across many partially-passing methods, and willingness to rearchitect (e.g. parser strategy, build-vs-reuse) when an approach stalls.

dimensions.name: Understanding the LSP contract & golden output format
dimensions.description: Reading run_tests.*, inspecting golden.jsonl structure, and reverse-engineering the exact JDT-LS response shape per LSP method before/while committing to an implementation.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The contract is under-specified prose; the real spec lives implicitly in golden.jsonl and the JDT-LS behaviors it encodes. Every method's expected response format (ranges, URIs, 0- vs 1-indexing, capability negotiation) must be inferred correctly or all downstream work misses. Acting blind here guarantees wasted implementation.

anchors.0: Starts coding a parser/server with no inspection of golden.jsonl, run_tests, or the LSP methods actually exercised.
anchors.3: Skims the task text, maybe opens golden.jsonl once; guesses response shapes and the set of methods rather than deriving them.
anchors.5: Reads run_tests and golden.jsonl, enumerates which methods and files are tested, and infers the basic response schema for the common methods before building.
anchors.8: Systematically dissects golden.jsonl: catalogs every ($method) present, extracts concrete expected-response exemplars, and pins down subtle format details (position indexing, URI scheme, range boundaries, initialize/capabilities handshake) — building an explicit internal spec of the contract.
anchors.10: Treats the golden set as a reverse-engineering target: derives per-method invariants from multiple examples, cross-checks ambiguous cases against JDT-LS conventions, distinguishes format requirements from semantic requirements, and re-probes the data whenever a mismatch reveals a misunderstood contract detail — sustaining this inquiry across the whole build.

dimensions.name: Layering the build (lexer → parser → AST → analysis → per-method handlers)
dimensions.description: Breaking an enormous surface into an ordered hierarchy — protocol plumbing, parsing, symbol model, then method-by-method handlers — each with a concrete done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With Java's grammar, semantic analysis, and many LSP methods, an undifferentiated push collapses. Sequencing (get stdio+initialize handshake working first, then a parseable AST, then the cheapest-to-pass methods) is what lets progress accumulate over a long horizon instead of stalling everywhere at once.

anchors.0: One monolithic attempt; no sub-goals, no ordering — tries to make everything work at once.
anchors.3: Vague mental split (‘parser then handlers’) with no explicit milestones or completion criteria per stage.
anchors.5: Identifies the main layers and a sensible order, tackles methods one at a time, and knows when a layer minimally works (e.g. handshake responds, files parse).
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy: protocol layer, parser, symbol table, then a prioritized method sequence chosen by dependency and cost-to-pass; each milestone has a concrete check (e.g. ‘hover passes on file X’) and later methods build on validated earlier ones.
anchors.10: Milestones are sequenced by leverage and risk — foundational/shared capabilities first, riskiest grammar or resolution work de-risked early with spikes, method groups batched by shared machinery — and the plan is revisited as passing counts reveal where remaining value concentrates.

dimensions.name: Driving development with the golden test loop and finer checks
dimensions.description: Deliberately using run_tests as the outer loop plus building tighter per-method / per-file diagnostics to localize failures beyond the aggregate score.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Success is defined by matching JDT-LS output exactly, so the agent must design how it learns of correctness: not just running run_tests, but diffing expected-vs-actual responses to see WHICH field/position is wrong. Without finer checks, a many-method server gives a single opaque pass rate and debugging becomes guesswork.

anchors.0: Never runs run_tests, or runs it once and assumes correctness from code inspection.
anchors.3: Runs run_tests occasionally as a pass/fail number with no per-case diffing; can't say which method or field fails.
anchors.5: Uses run_tests as a regular feedback loop and inspects failing cases to understand at least which methods are failing.
anchors.8: Builds a tight verification workflow: diffs expected vs actual per triple, isolates single methods/files, and adds targeted checks (e.g. feeding one request manually over stdio) to pinpoint the exact divergent field or position.
anchors.10: Engineers verification as infrastructure: structured expected-vs-actual diffing, regression guarding so fixed methods stay fixed, minimal reproduction of individual failing requests, and validation that passes reflect genuine analysis rather than coincidental format matches — sustained across the whole test suite.

dimensions.name: Tracking pass-rate across many methods without losing the plot
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate done-vs-remaining picture (which methods/files pass, which regressed) and detecting when stuck circling one failure.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With many methods and a large codebase, it's easy to churn on one stubborn case while regressing others, or to lose track of overall standing. Accurate accounting across the long horizon decides whether the agent converges toward all-tests-pass or thrashes.

anchors.0: No sense of overall standing; doesn't know how many/which cases pass at any point.
anchors.3: Vague awareness of the aggregate number; no per-method breakdown; doesn't notice regressions.
anchors.5: Tracks which methods pass vs fail and notices when the count moves the wrong way after a change.
anchors.8: Keeps a live, per-method/per-file ledger of pass state, detects regressions promptly, and recognizes when repeated edits to one failure aren't moving the needle — then redirects effort.
anchors.10: Maintains a disciplined progress model across the whole horizon: prioritizes remaining work by expected gain, catches thrash/circular-debugging early and explicitly steps back, and never loses sight of the global ‘all tests pass’ target while working local failures.

dimensions.name: Rearchitecting when the parser/analysis approach stalls
dimensions.description: Revising design decisions (parsing strategy, symbol model, build-vs-reuse) when evidence shows the current approach can't reach correctness, instead of grinding on it.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A hand-rolled recursive-descent Java parser or a naive symbol model may prove inadequate for the grammar or resolution the golden cases demand. The horizon is long enough that a wrong foundational bet is fatal unless the agent recognizes falsification and changes course.

anchors.0: Sticks rigidly to the first approach even as failures pile up; repeats the same fix attempts.
anchors.3: Makes only local patches to a failing design; never questions the foundational approach.
anchors.5: When an approach clearly isn't working, tries a materially different tactic for that piece rather than repeating the same edit.
anchors.8: Recognizes when a foundational choice (parser structure, resolution model, response serialization) is the root cause, and deliberately reworks it — updating dependent milestones — rather than layering hacks.
anchors.10: Treats divergence as signal: diagnoses the true root cause from failing evidence, weighs alternative architectures (including build-vs-reuse pivots), executes a clean rework while preserving already-passing behavior, and documents why the pivot beats persistence — repeatedly and decisively across the build.

dimensions.name: Build-vs-reuse and effort allocation across a huge surface
dimensions.description: Strategic decisions about what to implement by hand vs leverage from the ecosystem (e.g. a Java grammar/parser crate, an LSP/JSON-RPC framework) given finite effort against an enormous scope.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reimplementing the full Java grammar and LSP plumbing from scratch may be infeasible in-horizon; a skilled agent explicitly decides where to spend effort and where to stand on existing crates, while the task still demands genuine AST-based analysis. This allocation choice is high-leverage and distinct from mere sequencing.

anchors.0: No consideration of scope vs effort; blindly hand-builds everything (or reaches for nothing) with no rationale.
anchors.3: Makes an implicit build/reuse choice without weighing the trade-off or the task's ‘analyze the AST’ requirement.
anchors.5: Consciously decides which parts to hand-build vs pull from crates, with a basic rationale that respects the ‘real LSP’ constraint.
anchors.8: Deliberately allocates effort: leverages robust ecosystem pieces for plumbing/parsing where sound, concentrates hand-built effort on the analysis that earns test passes, and revisits the choice when a dependency proves limiting.
anchors.10: Makes and re-evaluates a coherent leverage strategy that maximizes coverage per unit effort while keeping the solution a genuine AST-analyzing server — choosing tools by fit to the golden contract and pivoting deliberately when a chosen tool blocks progress.

dimensions.name: Keeping the solution a real LSP, not a golden lookup
dimensions.description: Maintaining and self-checking that the server answers by analyzing the AST generally, rather than memorizing/retrieving golden.jsonl answers — the explicitly forbidden shortcut.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec explicitly bars using golden.jsonl as a retrieval layer and demands a real LSP. Passing tests via memorization is illusory progress; a skilled agent guards against this both as a design commitment and by sanity-checking that passes come from genuine analysis.

anchors.0: Hardcodes or looks up golden.jsonl responses; ‘passing’ is pure memorization.
anchors.3: Mostly general but slips in case-specific shortcuts/special-casing to force particular golden cases to pass.
anchors.5: Commits to a genuinely general AST-based approach and avoids retrieval, though without much explicit self-verification of generality.
anchors.8: Actively keeps the solution general and checks that passes stem from real analysis (e.g. reasoning about untested inputs, avoiding per-example special-casing), treating any memorization temptation as a red flag.
anchors.10: Holds a clear principle that the server must generalize, deliberately validates that its analysis would hold on inputs outside the golden set, and refactors away any accidental overfitting — ensuring measured progress reflects a real language server.
